title: Ebola Outbreak Tops 8,700 Cases as Kenya Confirms First Imported Infection
excerpt: The DRC's Bundibugyo outbreak is now the country's worst on record at 8,728 cases and 4,205 deaths — and MSF says North Kivu is becoming its new, uncontrollable center.
body:
• The World Health Organization says the DRC's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak reached 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 deaths as of October 6 — a 48.2% fatality rate — making it the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country and the second-largest anywhere.
  • Kenya confirmed its first imported case on October 6: a Kenyan man who lived in the DRC for seven years flew from Kampala to Nairobi on October 3 and died at Nairobi Hospital on October 5; 11 family members are quarantined and 23 healthcare workers are being followed up.
  • MSF warns North Kivu is becoming the new epicenter, accounting for nearly 40% of all new cases, with treatment centers stretched beyond capacity and over 60% of deaths still occurring in communities.
  • There is still no approved vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain: two candidates — an Oxford vaccine and a Moderna candidate — began early human trials in Uganda this week, while the standard Ervebo shot is being used only under compassionate-use protocols.

The Numbers Keep Climbing

The Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ebola outbreak is now the worst the country has ever faced. In its latest disease-outbreak bulletin, the World Health Organization reported 8,728 confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease and 4,205 confirmed deaths as of October 6, 2026 — a crude case-fatality ratio of 48.2%. The outbreak has reached 64 health zones across seven of the DRC's 26 provinces, and has now expanded to Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu, widening its geographic footprint.

https://x.com/sholard_mancity/status/2108384455308243266

Transmission remains intense nationally, the WHO said, though the picture is uneven. Some areas show signs the epidemic is slowing; others are accelerating. Over the three completed epidemiological weeks before the report, new weekly cases rose 2.5%, from 475 to 487, and new weekly deaths held steady at 224. A grim statistic underscores the struggle: of 372 deaths reported since the WHO's September 25 bulletin, 264 occurred in communities, not treatment centers — a sign patients are reaching care late or not at all.

North Kivu: "Like Fighting a Megafire"

The most alarming shift is geographic. North Kivu province, which accounted for just 24% of new cases at the end of August, now produces nearly 40% of them, according to Doctors Without Borders. New hotspots are emerging every week, and treatment capacity is buckling.

"It is like fighting a megafire. Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations. As long as new hotspots continue to emerge while the virus spreads across northern North Kivu, containing the epidemic will remain extremely difficult."

— Stéphanie Hoffmann, MSF Ebola treatment centre coordinator, Butembo

As of September 28, 34% of confirmed Ebola patients were being treated in non-specialized health facilities, MSF said, because dedicated treatment centers are full and diagnosis is delayed. Many of those facilities lack the resources and expertise for Ebola case management, raising the risk of transmission to other patients and healthcare workers. "Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community," Hoffmann said. Butembo health zone — home to an estimated two million people — had only two dedicated Ebola treatment centers until recently; two more have opened, but MSF says substantial investment is still needed.

Kenya's Imported Case

On October 7, Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale moved to calm nerves: the country's first confirmed case was imported, not the start of a domestic outbreak. "We don't have an Ebola outbreak in Kenya. What we have is an imported Ebola incident, just like the same happened in Germany and in France," Duale said in a televised interview.

The patient, a Kenyan who had lived in the DRC for seven years, fell ill after contracting the disease there, traveled overland to Kampala, and flew into Nairobi on Jambojet flight 8523 on October 3. Heavy medication suppressed his fever, helping him slip through thermal screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. He was taken directly to Nairobi Hospital, where doctors noticed high fever, chills, and difficulty swallowing; he was isolated and died at about 11:30 pm on October 5.

Contact tracing began immediately across Kenya, Uganda, and the DRC with WHO support. Eleven members of the patient's family, including his mother and wife, were placed under quarantine; 23 healthcare workers who interacted with him are being followed up, along with the four crew members from his flight and airport staff who may have had contact. Kenya has screened about 650,000 passengers at 15 points of entry and trained 4,900 healthcare workers for Ebola response.

No Vaccine Yet — But Trials Are Starting

The Bundibugyo strain is especially dangerous because no specifically approved vaccine or treatment exists for it. The standard Ervebo vaccine, approved only against the Zaire strain, is being administered under compassionate-use protocols as the only available option. This week brought the first real hope: the University of Oxford's ChAdOx1 BDBV vaccine began Phase Ib trials in Uganda on October 6, and a Moderna candidate received ethical approval on October 7 — both having completed earlier safety trials in the UK and Canada.

The WHO declared the Bundibugyo outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on May 17, 2026. Its risk assessment rates the threat as very high within the DRC, high for neighboring countries sharing land borders, and low regionally and globally. Uganda's own outbreak was declared over on July 28, and one imported case each has been reported in France and in a US citizen medically evacuated to Germany.

What Comes Next

The next weeks will test two fronts at once: whether North Kivu's treatment capacity can be scaled fast enough to catch new hotspots, and whether Kenya's rapid response — with the WHO supplying diagnostic kits and protective equipment — can keep an imported case from becoming a chain. MSF is calling for urgent mobilization of treatment capacity across the province, warning that without community trust and early care-seeking, the megafire keeps spreading.

nri_angle: For the diaspora traveling to East and Central Africa or with family there, the key facts are concrete: Kenya's case was imported and contained with quarantine and tracing in place, the WHO rates global risk as low, and the vaccine trials now underway in Uganda are the first real path to a Bundibugyo-specific vaccine.
